questions.q: Why does this ride-sharing platform need two separate freshness SLAs rather than one?
options: Driver location must stay under 10 seconds stale for matching, while trip analytics can tolerate 15 minutes — two different consumers with different needs
Freshness SLAs must always be identical across an entire platform
Only trip events need a freshness SLA; location pings need none
SLAs are only relevant to batch processing, not streaming
questions.explain: Two requirements on the same platform mean one processing model and one SLA can't cleanly serve both.

questions.q: Why do driver location pings and trip events need two different storage paths?
options: Location pings need a low-latency store answering "where is this driver right now," while trip events need a durable, replayable store like Delta Lake for historical analytics
Both signals should always be stored in exactly the same table
Trip events don't need to be stored at all
Location pings are always stored in the same star schema as trip events
questions.explain: One needs live lookup, not history scanning; the other needs durability and replayability for BI and Kappa reprocessing.

questions.q: How does Kappa architecture apply to this platform's single streaming pipeline?
options: The same pipeline both updates the live surge multiplier and durably lands events in Delta Lake for replay, avoiding a separate batch job
Kappa requires two completely separate pipelines for live and historical processing
Kappa architecture cannot be applied to ride-sharing data
The surge multiplier is always computed by a nightly batch job instead
questions.explain: One streaming pipeline serves both live matching and historical/replay needs, exactly as Lesson 7 described.

questions.q: Why does the trip fact table get partitioned by date and city?
options: Because almost every analytical query on trips filters by one or both of those dimensions
Partitioning by date and city is required by Delta Lake regardless of query patterns
Trip fact tables should never be partitioned
Date and city partitioning is unrelated to query performance
questions.explain: Partitioning aligns with how the data is actually queried, per Lesson 9's partitioning strategy.

questions.q: Why does the live location store need to be sharded by geohash or city?
options: So a launch-day surge in one city doesn't overwhelm a single shard and slow down matching everywhere
Sharding location data is unnecessary at any scale
Geohash sharding is only useful for trip analytics, not live matching
One shard can handle unlimited location ping volume from every city
questions.explain: Without sharding, a hot city becomes a hot spot that degrades matching performance platform-wide.
